summary: A 1980 list of assigned numbers used in network protocols. It replaced RFC 758 and was replaced by RFC 770. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC collects number assignments used by network protocols in January 1980. Its tables show which values had been assigned to networks, protocols, services, and links.

questions: what is an internet protocol number
subtitle: The January 1980 list of assigned numbers used by network protocols.

tldr.problem: Protocol implementations needed coordinated values for network identifiers, protocol types, ports or sockets, and links.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC compiles then-current assignments into tables and directs developers who need a number to contact the person maintaining assignments.
tldr.outcome: It documented the assignments available at that time and was later replaced by RFC 770.

today: RFC 762 is Historic and was replaced by RFC 770. It preserves the assignments listed in the January 1980 registry.

sections.title: Purpose of the Assigned-Numbers List
sections.content:
RFC 762 records assigned values from several number series used in network protocol implementations. The RFC says the list would be updated periodically and asks developers who need a link, socket, or other number assignment to contact Jon Postel.

The tables cover network numbers, Internet Protocol versions, Internet Protocol numbers, port or socket numbers, and link numbers. The document also points readers to references for the listed protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC brings several sets of network number assignments together in one place. Developers were directed to request new assignments from the person managing them.

sections.title: Networks and Protocol Identifiers
sections.content:
The registry lists network numbers in an 8-bit field, protocol versions in a 4-bit field, and Internet Protocol numbers in an 8-bit field. Its entries identify named networks and protocol types, while also marking values as reserved or unassigned.

For example, the table assigns network number 10 to ARPANET, version number 4 to the August 1979 Internet Protocol version, and protocol number 17 to User Datagram.
sections.plainLanguage: Different fields use numbers to identify networks, protocol versions, and the next protocol carried by Internet Protocol. The tables mark which values already had names and which were still available or reserved.

sections.title: Service and Link Numbers
sections.content:
The port or socket section explains that these numbers name contact points for services or logical connections. It lists ranges for network-wide standard functions, host-specific functions, future use, and experiments, followed by assignments such as Echo, Date and Time, and Name Server.

The link section describes how the term “link” relates to the high-order 8 bits of a 12-bit message-ID field in the Host/IMP interface. Its table lists uses including control messages, regular messages, Internet Protocol, measurements, and experimental protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: The list assigns numbers to network services and to message categories called links. Each table explains what its number field identifies and records the values assigned at the time.

sections.title: Status of This Registry
sections.content: The RFC says the assigned-numbers document would be updated periodically. The unit metadata records RFC 770 as the document that replaced RFC 762.
sections.plainLanguage: This registry is a snapshot of assignments from January 1980. RFC 770 later replaced it.

references.text: Postel, J., "User Datagram Protocol", IEN-88, May 1979.
